body_markdown:
Anthropic is now a public company trading on Nasdaq under ANT. As it moves from private market promises to public market accountability, enterprises get something valuable: a quarterly view of whether frontier AI economics will work, better transparency and more buying power.


In[June](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/anthropics-proposed-ipo-will-change-the-economics-of-enterprise-ai/) , we argued that public markets would impose discipline and expected pricing to get more realistic, capital to fuel expansion/acquisitions, and economics to push Anthropic toward greater cost efficiency. In[October](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/anthropics-s-1-hands-enterprise-ai-buyers-better-leverage/) , the S-1 exposed Anthropic’s economic bind: Its newest models drove revenue, founders kept unusual control, and massive compute commitments made utilization, not just margins — the central test. Third-quarter revenue rose 47% to $17billion, but compute and infrastructure costs climbed to 58% of revenue from 48%, and a $974 million second-quarter operating profit became a $567 million loss.


The real test begins now: Can Anthropic turn demand for AI into durable AI economics? Can Anthropic revolutionize all knowledge work? Can Anthropic achieve this sustainably? What will this mean for the future of enterprise AI? Today’s IPO adds a ticker symbol that literally and figuratively can carry a lot of weight for enterprise AI buyers.


## **Your AI Workloads (And The Value They Create) Will Be The Real Prize**


Anthropic’s economics increasingly resemble a volume business: Large compute commitments create pressure to grow consumption, even as routing, caching, and smaller models lower serving costs. As more enterprise tasks shift to cheaper models, frontier capabilities may concentrate on higher-value work. The challenge is turning rising usage and falling unit costs into profitable revenue and sufficient returns on invested capital. That gives Anthropic a powerful incentive to win more enterprise workloads, agents, coding tasks, and business processes, not just to drive volume, but to make that volume pay.


**What it means:** Anthropic needs your workloads nearly as much as you need its intelligence but must grow consumption without sacrificing margins. Use that tension as leverage: Negotiate on cost per completed task, not just token prices, and seek volume discounts, model-upgrade terms, flexible usage limits, benchmark-based pricing reopeners, rollover of unused commitments, guaranteed model-support periods, and uptime-linked service credits. Cloud marketplaces account for 48% of Anthropic’s revenue, giving many buyers leverage through existing AWS, Google, or Microsoft spend commitments; its top five customers contributed about 25% of revenue in the first nine months of the year, underscoring the importance of large enterprise relationships.


## **The Frontier Race Will Not Slow**


Don’t assume public market discipline means Anthropic will prioritize efficiency over innovation. They will prioritize both. Anthropic’s S-1 says models released in the six months to September 30 this year, generated more than 80% of its third-quarter revenue. Anthropic doesn’t just need good models. It needs a steady stream of new good models and will continue to innovate on this front. Wield the power of these innovative models to build your own competitive AI advantage.


**What it means:** Expect faster model turnover, not stability. Keep another frontier platform production-ready and design contracts and architecture to make switching easier. You need a[dual vendor frontier strategy](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/anthropics-founders-letter-has-the-right-ideals-but-reality-will-decide/) . One is not enough. The frontier market is still extremely fluid: The hyperscalers are building their own frontier model platforms, open weights keep closing the gap, and pricing and usage policies change by the quarter.


## **Enterprises Will Buy Platforms, Not Models**


Remember when enterprises chose AI providers by comparing models: Which has the largest context window? Lowest token costs? Best answers? These questions still matter, but not in isolation. Buyers must now evaluate models against the value of the task, the enterprise data available, the agents they power and the company’s broader model strategy.


**What it means:** As agents orchestrate work across applications, data, and people, frontier AI is becoming the next operating system for enterprise software, helping you automate workflows faster than your competitors. Buyers must scrutinize not just its intelligence but the risks beneath it. Can you switch providers if a platform fails? What does the SLA pay out, and will Anthropic publish outage postmortems? Can you move your agents, prompts, and data elsewhere? Above all, have you tested your AI business continuity and disaster recovery plans? Treat resilience, portability, security, and governance as core buying criteria, especially in the backdrop of the[tech outages](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/the-microsoft-outage-demands-an-end-to-vendor-concentration-risk-and-a-commitment-to-resilience/) and[network modernization failure](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/the-faa-ground-stop-shows-why-network-transformation-must-be-engineered-for-failure/) events from last week.
